title: Shemot: the lost lamb (Exodus Rabbah 2:2)
hook: midrash: Moses carries a runaway lamb back, and God chooses him to shepherd a people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: the book of Exodus begins with names, and the midwives are remembered while Pharaoh isn't. Your line was start with the names. Did you learn one? Today, Moses, grown up, far from Egypt, with a flock. Day two hundred twenty-two.

How do you pick a leader? A job interview. A résumé. A vote, a speech, a debate. We look for the big moments. The Torah tells us Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew slave, fled to the desert, married, and became a shepherd for his father-in-law, Jethro. Then, one day, God speaks to him from a burning bush and sends him to free a nation. The Torah doesn't say why him. The rabbis wanted to know. So they told a story about an ordinary afternoon with the sheep.
screen: `HOW DO YOU PICK A LEADER?` → `PALACE, DESERT, SHEPHERD.` → `THE TORAH DOESN'T SAY WHY.`

segments.voice: The story is a midrash, a rabbinic teaching that fills a gap in the text, and it's in a collection called Exodus Rabbah. Here it is. Moses is tending Jethro's flock in the wilderness. One little animal slips away and runs. The midrash actually says a young goat; it's usually retold as a lamb. Moses goes after it. It runs and runs, until it reaches a shady spot with a pool of water, and stops to drink. And Moses, out of breath, standing there, says: I didn't know you were running because you were thirsty. You must be exhausted. And he picks it up, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it all the way back to the flock. That's the whole story. No miracle. No speech. And the midrash says God saw it and said: you have compassion to lead a flock that belongs to a man. By your life, you will shepherd my flock, Israel. Notice what Moses didn't do. He didn't scold the runaway. He didn't leave it; it was one animal out of many. He assumed the running had a reason, and the reason was need. The same midrash tells a similar story about David, the shepherd boy who became king: he let the youngest sheep eat the tender grass first. In this telling, you don't find a leader on a stage. You find one in the moment nobody is watching, when somebody small wanders off, and someone goes after them.
screen: `A MIDRASH FILLS A GAP.` · `THE RUNAWAY WAS THIRSTY.` · `CARRIED HOME ON HIS SHOULDERS.` · `NOW SHEPHERD MY FLOCK.` · then, large: `CARRY THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back for someone left behind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has drifted away from a group you're part of. The friend who stopped coming. The relative who went quiet. The classmate who's always a few steps behind. Instead of wondering what's wrong with them, ask Moses's question: what are they thirsty for? Then decide one small way to go after them. The bell holds the time.
Shemot. The portion where Moses, a shepherd in the desert, is chosen to lead; a midrash says it was because he carried back a runaway lamb.
Your line: carry the lamb. Today, reach out to one person who has drifted away, and assume they had a reason. Day two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls Moses Moshe Rabbeinu, Moses our teacher, and often calls him the faithful shepherd; midrashim like this one are taught to children and adults alike to explain what the Torah leaves unsaid.

chase it, and carry it back.
fork.reveal: in the midrash, Moses chased it to a pool, realized it was thirsty, and carried it home on his shoulders. God chose him to shepherd Israel.

original.note: Hebrew: shepherd. What Moses was when God called him, and what the midrash says he became for a people.

what a scholar hears: Exodus Rabbah 2:2 pairs Moses with David, both tested as shepherds before they led Israel.
